newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Israel under fire at U.N. for E.Jerusalem building.
newsitem.headline: Israel under fire at U.N. for E.Jerusalem building.

text.p: The United States criticised Israel on Wednesday for its decision to build a new Jewish neighbourhood in mainly Arab East Jerusalem but said the Security Council should not take any action that would hamper future Middle East peace negotiations.

American U.N. envoy Bill Richardson was taking part in a council debate on a widely criticised Israeli plan to build 6,500 homes for Jews on a tree-covered hill between East Jerusalem and Bethlehem called Har Homa by Israel and Jabal Abu Ghneim by the Palestinians.

"The United States is concerned by the decision announced by the Israeli governmenmt. We do not believe such activity is helpful to the peace process," he said, echoing remarks made in Washington earlier this week by President Bill Clinton.

But Richardson said that, when "permanent status" negotiations on a range of difficult issues were due to resume soon, "we should not take any action that would detract from this objective and which could make the tasks of the parties that much more difficult."

Opening the debate, the Palestine Liberation Organisation's U.N. observer, Nasser al-Kidwa, called on the council to prevent Israel from building "colonial settlements" in East Jerusalem and other parts of the territories occupied since the 1967 Middle East war.

"We believe that the Security Council has to intervene and take the necessary action in a clear resolution to guarantee respect for its relevant resolutions, for international law and to save the peace process," he said.

A few hours before the debate began, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, who visited Washington earlier in the week, held an informal meeting with council members to press his case and stress the need for the council to ensure the Middle East peace process remained on track.
Israeli U.N. envoy David Peleg expressed regret the council was discussing a contentious issue which, according to past agreements between Israel and the Palestinians, should be settled between them.

He said building in Jerusalem did not constitute a change in the city's status and would not affect negotiations on "final status" issues but was part of a plan to alleviate a housing shortage for both Jews and Arabs.
He said 75 percent of the land for the Har Homa project was owned by individual Jews and that 3,000 housing units would be built in 10 predominantly Arab Jerusalem neighbourhoods.
A large number of speakers were taking part in the council debate, due to continue on Thursday, and almost all were critical of Israel in varying degrees.
Al-Kidwa said Israel's policies and measures "cannot continue if the peace process is to continue and succeed."

He said the council had repeatedly affirmed that the Fourth Geneva Convention on the protection of civilians in time of war, which bars settlements in occupied territory, applied to all areas occupied by Israel since 1967, including Jerusalem.

Britain's Sir John Weston said it was "not too late for the Israeli government to suspend, or even rescind, its decision in principle to go ahead with Har Homa." If it showed signs it was "willing to change its hard line stance, we would be willing to consider a delay to council reaction," he added.
Ambassador Sergei Lavrov of Russia said Israeli settlements would be emphasised during a forthcoming visit to Moscow by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

No resolution has yet been circulated. But the European Union members of the Security Council are working on a draft calling on Israel to "refrain from all actions or measures ... which alter the facts on the ground, pre-empt the final status negotiations, and have negative implications for the Middle East peace process."
It would also call on Israel to abide scrupulously by its obligations under the Fourth Geneva Convention and urge all parties to press ahead with the peace process.
